name: itoa (integer-to-string)
baseline: std's Display for integers (format!, to_string, write!)
verdict_reason: itoa publishes its results only as a chart, so the size of its lead cannot be quoted. Since Rust 1.98 (2026-08-20) std has core::fmt::NumBuffer and integer format_into, which call the same internal digit routine (_fmt_inner) straight into a stack buffer and skip Formatter, the overhead itoa exists to avoid. No published benchmark compares itoa with format_into.
tier_reason: Numbers exist only in a chart image (itoa README and itoa-benchmark).
claimed_speedup: No numbers in text. itoa-benchmark shows a chart only, measured on a 2025 AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9975WX using Rust 1.92.0.
workload: Random u32, u64 and u128 values with equal counts per type and digit length; fastest pass per group.
one_liner: Integer-to-decimal formatting without core::fmt::Formatter; std 1.98's NumBuffer::format_into now offers the same path built in.
how_it_is_fast: Uses libcore's own two-digits-at-a-time lookup-table routine but writes into a fixed stack Buffer and returns &str, skipping the Formatter machinery (padding, flags, dynamic dispatch through fmt::Write).
use_it_when: Toolchains older than 1.98, where std has no Formatter-free integer API
Libraries with an MSRV below 1.98 (itoa's MSRV is 1.68)
skip_it_when: Rust 1.98 or later: try core::fmt::NumBuffer with {integer}::format_into first
Code that formats a handful of integers, where Formatter overhead does not matter
caveats: Chart-only results; no text numbers to quote
Benchmark run on Rust 1.92.0, before NumBuffer was stable; std's format_into was not measured
Benchmark is maintained by itoa's author and builds with -C target-cpu=native
tradeoffs: Another dependency for something std now covers on 1.98+

evidence.quote: The implementation comes straight from [libcore] but avoids the performance penalty of going through [`core::fmt::Formatter`].
The following results are measured on a 2025 AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9975WX using Rust 1.92.0.
A buffer wrapper of which the internal size is based on the maximum number of digits the associated integer can have.
